Sacrilegious
săk-rĭ-lē´jŭs
adj. (violating what is sacred; robbing holy things; rendering Greek hierosuleo, to commit sacrilege)
Latin sacrilegus, from sacer, sacred, and legere, to gather or steal — literally a temple-robber. The Greek hierosulos is the same picture.

Biblical Definition

To be sacrilegious is to lay hands on what belongs to God. Paul presses the charge on the man who boasts of the law: “Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?” (Rom 2:22). The town clerk at Ephesus certified that Paul's companions were “neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess” (Act 19:37). Achan took of the accursed thing and Israel could not stand before her enemies (Jos 7:11–12). Belshazzar drank from the temple vessels and the writing came out on the wall that night (Dan 5:3–5). Malachi puts it as a question: “Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me” (Mal 3:8).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines sacrilegious as violating sacred things; polluted with the crime of sacrilege; profane; impious.

expand to see more

SACRILEGIOUS, a. Violating sacred things; polluted with the crime of sacrilege.

2. Containing sacrilege; partaking of the crime of sacrilege; profane; impious.

Key Scripture

Rom 2:22 — "Thou that sayest a man should not commit adultery, dost thou commit adultery? thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?"

Mal 3:8 — "Will a man rob God? Yet ye have robbed me. But ye say, Wherein have we robbed thee? In tithes and offerings."

Dan 5:3 — "Then they brought the golden vessels that were taken out of the temple of the house of God which was at Jerusalem; and the king, and his princes, his wives, and his concubines, drank in them."

Jos 7:11 — "Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff."

Act 19:37 — "For ye have brought hither these men, which are neither robbers of churches, nor yet blasphemers of your goddess."

Modern Corruption

Sacrilege is imagined as vandalism in a cathedral, and Malachi charges it against men who kept back a tithe.

expand to see more

Malachi 3:8 asks the question in the plainest possible form — will a man rob God? — and answers it against a congregation that was still attending, still sacrificing, and still asking wherein have we robbed thee. The answer given is tithes and offerings: not a smashed altar, not a stolen vessel, but a withheld portion. Sacrilege in Scripture is far more often a quiet subtraction than a violent act, and the men charged with it are usually inside the building.

Romans 2:22 finds the same thing in a subtler place. Paul is addressing the Jew who abhors idols — genuinely, on principle — and asks whether he commits sacrilege, probably of trafficking in what had been devoted to idols, certainly of profiting from what he claimed to detest. The pattern is permanent: a religion strict in its condemnations and loose about what it takes. Belshazzar's feast is the same sin without the hypocrisy, and it was the last hour of his kingdom.

The doctrine under all of it is that God has property. He devoted Jericho, He owns the tithe, He claims the vessels, He calls a day His own and a body His temple — “if any man defile the temple of God, him shall God destroy; for the temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” (1Co 3:17). The modern reader who finds the whole category strange has usually stopped believing that anything is set apart, which is the condition in which sacrilege becomes invisible rather than impossible.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hierosuleo (G2416), to rob temples, commit sacrilege; hierosulos (G2417), a temple-robber; Hebrew cherem (H2764), the devoted or accursed thing; qaba (H6906), to rob.

expand to see more

Greek hierosuleo (G2416) — to commit sacrilege; Romans 2:22 only; hierosulos (G2417), Acts 19:37 only.

Hebrew cherem (H2764) — the devoted thing, accursed; Joshua 6:18, 7:1, 7:11–13.

Hebrew qaba (H6906) — to rob, defraud; Malachi 3:8–9, Proverbs 22:23.

Usage

"“Will a man rob God?” — asked of men who were still attending."

"“Thou that abhorrest idols, dost thou commit sacrilege?” — strict in condemnation, loose in taking."

"“The temple of God is holy, which temple ye are” — the property in question now."
